newsitem.title: USA: Smoker's deposition read at Reynolds trial.
newsitem.headline: Smoker's deposition read at Reynolds trial.

text.p: In a deposition taken before her death, smoker Jean Connor said she believed some cigarette advertising was banned because smoking was a health hazard.

A representative of R.J. Reynolds Tobacco Co on Wednesday read parts of Connor's deposition into the record at a wrongful death trial, apparently to bolster the cigarette maker's key contention that Connor chose to smoke despite knowing of the potential health risks.
Connor's sister, Dana Raulerson, sued the company in Florida on behalf of Connor's estate and her three children.
Connor developed a heavy smoking habit as a teen-ager and eventually smoked three packs a day, quitting shortly before she died of lung cancer in 1995 at age 49.

In parts of her deposition read to the jury, Connor said she was addicted to cigarettes and conceded that she had never participated in the Great American Smokeout -- a day when smokers do without cigarettes -- because "I didn't want to."
In answer to a question about why some cigarette advertising is banned, Connor said it was because "smoking was hazardous to my health."

Asked why she had not heeded health warnings on cigarette labels, Connor said: "It said they may be hazardous. It didn't say they would definitely be hazardous." She also said the labels did not specify what type of hazard.
Reynolds representatives also read into the record parts of depositions from Connor's son, Matthew Marion, her ex-husband, Donald Connor, and her mother, Margaret Thomas.
The son, 23, a smoker who began at age 17, said his mother would not let him smoke in front of her. "She told me it was bad for me and I should quit," he said.

After Jean Connor quit smoking in 1993 because she wanted to have plastic surgery and the surgeon would not perform the procedure while she smoked, Connor again told her son to quit, his deposition said.
"I did it; you ought to do it," the son said his mother told him.

Donald Connor, a chain smoker who was married to Jean Connor from 1979 to 1980 and again from 1981 to 1984, said it was clear that cigarettes affected Connor health, especially when she was dancing and found it hard to breathe.
"These things are killing me," Donald Connor recalled Jean Connor saying.
Margaret Thomas, in her deposition, said she had told her children not to smoke. "I wish you would never, ever smoke or drink because I hate both of them," she recalled saying.

The depositions appeared to be aimed at supporting testimony on Tuesday from University of South Carolina historian Lacy Ford, who said the potential risks of cigarette smoking were common knowledge in the 1950s and 1960s -- the time Connor began smoking.

Lawyers for Raulerson also read some of Connor's deposition in which she talked about how she had tried switching from Salem to Salem Lights but they did not satisfy her craving. Salem cigarettes are made by Reynolds.
"You get this craving where you need to smoke a cigarette," said Connor, adding that she would go out in snowstorms when she lived in Massachusetts to get cigarettes because the urge was so strong.
Reynolds, a unit of RJR Nabisco Holdings Corp, was expected to rest its case late Wednesday after calling its final witness, Domenic Ciraulo, a Boston University psychiatrist and expert on addiction.
Judge Bernard Nachman has tentatively scheduled closing arguments for Friday morning and indicated he could decide to have the jury deliberate on Saturday if no verdict was reached Friday.
